Photograph: KIVI via Reuters Idaho Man who returned fire at In-N-Out gunman had done firearm training after 2021 mass shooting Police credited Jordan Salinas with limiting number of victims in attack on restaurant in Twin Falls, Idaho Edward Helmore Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.16 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A healthcare worker returning fire on a 24-year-old gunman who killed three people and wounded several others an In-N-Out Burger in Twin Falls, Idaho, has said his impulse to confront the attacker was “automatic” and “mechanical”. Shooting at In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Idaho leaves three people dead Read more That description from 35-year-old Jordan Salinas came in an interview with the Idaho Statesman that was published on Sunday, providing a detailed account of actions that police credited with limiting the number of victims in the attack a day earlier. Salinas said he was headed out for a horseback riding date with his girlfriend when they stopped at the burger restaurant for lunch at about 2.30pm on Saturday. Salinas saw people fleeing and heard the “pop-pop-pop” of gunfire, according to what he told the Statesman. He said he ran toward the sound in an “automatic” and “mechanical” response, drawing from a shoulder holster a semi-automatic pistol with a suppressor fixed to its barrel. Salinas said he had been training with firearms seriously since a deadly shooting at a mall in Boise, Idaho – about a two-hour drive from Twin Falls – left two dead and four wounded. And he said he watched on Saturday as an attacker later identified as Chad Williams, standing by the drive-through window, lifted a rifle to his shoulder and fired toward cars. Salinas countered by raising his pistol with both hands and firing. “He did not like it when bullets started firing both ways,” Salinas told the outlet. Police later said the attacker died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound, crediting Salinas and an off-duty officer for diverting the shooter with return fire. “We believe their actions helped drive the suspect away from the scene, preventing further casualties,” said Matthew Hicks, the Twin Falls police chief, at a news conference. “We want to take a moment and commend the actions of the off-duty officer and the citizen – and their heroic action to stop this incident.” Jack Johnson, the Twin Falls county sheriff, said: “These people are true heroes in our community. They diverted the shooter and without a doubt saved many lives.” Williams, 24, killed three victims before dying by his own hand, police said. Police added that he wounded seven others at the recently opened restaurant in the southern Idaho city of about 56,000 people. Two of the wounded were treated at a hospital and discharged; three were listed as stable; and two were in critical condition. Salinas – a full-time caregiver of his brother, who gets around in a wheelchair – said he felt “no fear” during the confrontation with Williams after following four steps he had learned in firearm training. Those steps, he said, were “observe, orient, decide [and] act”. “There’s a task that needs to be done, and we’re the ones who need to do it,” he told the outlet. The decision to take up firearms training, he said, came after he reasoned that gunmen go after “soft targets”. And a person in a wheelchair, and the aide at his side, would be exactly that, he said. “Everyone says, ‘It’s not going to happen here,’” Salinas said. “But what if it does?” Salinas’ interview and the police’s praise of him came amid a debate over the correct response of bystanders to mass shootings. Some witnesses to Saturday’s attack in Twin Falls were reported to have slowed their cars and shouted at Williams. As of Monday morning, there had been at least 280 mass shootings reported across the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive . The archive, a nonpartisan resource, defines mass shootings as cases in which four or more victims are shot or wounded. The high numbers of mass shootings annually reported in the US have driven calls for more substantial federal firearms restrictions. But Congress has not implemented such gun control over the years. https://bmmagazine.co.uk/business/one-hu.text: Lithuanian law allows a bank to freeze a suspicious transaction for a maximum of 10 business days without formal law-enforcement action. If your business account stays blocked longer than that, with no explanation and no evidence of a criminal investigation, courts have repeatedly ruled the freeze unlawful – and ordered the bank to return the funds plus interest. Revolut, the London-founded fintech, provides its European banking services through a subsidiary licensed in Lithuania and supervised by the Bank of Lithuania and the European Central Bank. It is there, in Vilnius, that a recent set of figures has drawn scrutiny – and with them a question that will be familiar to any British business following the UK’s own debate over frozen accounts: how long may a bank withhold a customer’s money before the law requires it to be returned? Rolandas Kiškis, head of Lithuania’s Financial Crime Investigation Service (FCIS – the country’s Financial Intelligence Unit), recently gave the Lithuanian Parliament’s Budget and Finance Committee a telling statistic: the agency receives around 100,000 suspicious transaction reports a year, and a striking 80% of them come from a single market player – Revolut Bank. As the FCIS head himself noted, most of these reports are generated automatically, by a system that files a report the moment it detects the faintest hint of risk. Revolut’s explanation is straightforward: the bank serves 57 million customers across the European Economic Area, so it naturally generates proportionally more reports, and its transaction monitoring relies on AI-driven systems that respond to potential fraud in real time. For a UK readership the relevance is twofold. Revolut is a British-founded company that many in the UK use, so how frozen funds are handled within its European operations is of natural interest. More practically, a large number of UK businesses operating across the Channel – those with EU subsidiaries, euro-denominated accounts or European customers – hold money with institutions licensed not by the FCA but by regulators in Vilnius, Dublin or Amsterdam. Where such an account is frozen, it is the law of that jurisdiction, not UK law, that governs the customer’s rights. Anti-money laundering compliance is, without question, an important, legally mandated duty for financial institutions. But this statistic has another side, one rarely discussed in public: behind every automatically generated report there is often a real customer whose funds are frozen, whose account may be blocked, and who frequently receives no explanation for weeks, months, sometimes over a year. “In practice, a number of these situations have no legal basis at all, and courts are increasingly ruling in customers’ favour,” says Dr. Justinas Jarusevičius, a partner and attorney at Lithuanian law firm Motieka & Audzevičius. How Long Can a Bank Legally Freeze Your Money? The 10-Business-Day Rule Lithuania’s Law on the Prevention of Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing – the national implementation of the EU’s anti-money-laundering framework – sets out a clear mechanism. When a financial institution identifies a suspicious transaction, it must suspend it and report it to FCIS within three business hours (Art. 16). From that point, the decision shifts to the state. FCIS has 10 business days to take the steps needed to confirm or dispel its suspicions. If, within that period, the financial institution receives no instruction to apply a temporary restriction on ownership rights under the Code of Criminal Procedure, the transaction must be resumed. In other words, a customer’s funds can lawfully stay frozen over a suspicious transaction for longer than 10 business days only once law enforcement has become involved and applied criminal-procedure measures – measures that can themselves be challenged in court. In practice, Jarusevičius says, a different scenario often plays out: the financial institution blocks the account on its own initiative, tells the customer only that “compliance checks” are under way, or offers no explanation at all, while the funds sit “under review” for months – with no FCIS instruction, no pre-trial investigation, no court order. In such cases, if the institution cannot point to a specific legal basis, the freeze is unlawful and the institution faces civil liability. Who Has to Prove the Freeze Was Justified? What the Courts Have Ruled A telling example is a dispute recently concluded against NIUM EU, UAB, an electronic money institution licensed in Lithuania, in which Jarusevičius’s firm, Motieka & Audzevičius , represented two business clients. In June 2022, the institution cut off the clients’ access to accounts holding close to EUR 490,000, without any warning. Their complaints went unanswered, not within the 15-business-day deadline set by the Law on Payments, nor afterwards: the first substantive response arrived more than six months later, and the actual legal basis for freezing the funds was never disclosed until the case reached court. On 6 June 2024, the Vilnius Regional Court, in civil case No. e2-1187-643/2024, ruled that the institution had failed to prove any legal basis for withholding the clients’ funds. The court rejected the institution’s defence, which relied on an instruction from a UK regulator addressed to the institution’s sister company: that instruction was neither binding on the Lithuanian entity in its dealings with its own clients, nor did it cover the claimants, who had no contractual relationship with the entities named in it. It was also significant that nothing in the case showed FCIS had ever been informed about the clients’ transactions at all, meaning the statutory prevention mechanism had never even been triggered. On 12 December 2024, the Lithuanian Court of Appeal, in civil case No. e2A-510-912/2024, upheld the first instance ruling and set out a rule with significant practical implications: in disputes of this kind, it is the financial institution that must prove it reasonably restricted the client’s account access and had the right to withhold the funds. A vague reference to AML law, or to a generic contract clause allowing the institution to suspend services “in accordance with legal requirements” is not enough – the institution must identify and prove the specific statutory provision, or the specific instruction from a competent authority, underlying its actions. This Court of Appeal case is not an isolated one. Lithuanian courts are currently hearing a number of similar cases in which clients of Lithuania-licensed financial institutions are seeking the return of funds held in their accounts but frozen by those institutions. The outcome for the clients was not just the return of their funds (the institution transferred most of it once it learned of the court proceedings) – the court also awarded 12.5% annual interest for the period between the filing of the case and the return of the funds, plus legal costs. What Should a Customer Whose Funds Are Frozen Do? Jarusevičius recommends three practical steps. First, demand a written explanation of the grounds for the freeze. Under the Law on Payments, payment service providers must inform customers about the blocking of a payment instrument and its reasons (with narrow statutory exceptions), and must review a written complaint and provide a reasoned response within 15 business days. Second, track the timeline. If more than 10 business days have passed since the transaction was suspended and the customer has received no information about any measures taken by law enforcement, the continued freeze is likely without legal basis. Third, enforce your rights. Consumers can turn to the Bank of Lithuania, which resolves disputes between consumers and financial market participants out of court. For business clients, the main route is litigation, where they can claim not only the return of their funds but also interest for the period the funds were unlawfully withheld. The case law above shows that the burden of proof in these disputes falls on the financial institution, and that a passive stance by the institution, failing to respond to complaints, failing to disclose grounds, is weighed by courts in the client’s favour. Clients often ask whether they have to simply wait for the bank to act first. They don’t, Jarusevičius says. Once the 10-business-day window has passed with no sign of law-enforcement involvement, the customer can send a formal legal demand and, if that goes unanswered, file a claim – there is no requirement to keep waiting indefinitely for the institution to volunteer an explanation. Prevention – Yes. Arbitrariness – No. The problem is not the filing of suspicious activity reports itself – that is a statutory, socially useful duty, and a high volume of reports does not by itself indicate wrongdoing. The problem arises when risk management turns into the indefinite withholding of customer funds without legal basis, without information, and without law enforcement involvement. Lawmakers struck this balance clearly: a suspicion gives an institution the right to suspend a transaction for days, not months. After that, it is for the state to decide, and if it doesn’t, the money must go back to its owner. As the volume of automated reports keeps growing, that rule only becomes more relevant. For UK businesses that hold funds with EEA-licensed institutions, it is a distinction worth understanding before, not after, an account is frozen. Justinas Jarusevičius is an attorney representing clients in financial services litigation, including the case against NIUM EU, UAB described above. Photograph: Facebook Italy Woman, 45, killed in Florence in seventh alleged femicide in Italy since mid-August Lorena Isceri was thrown off a motorway bridge, allegedly by ex-boyfriend Federico Vella Angela Giuffrida in Rome Fri 4 Sep 2026 09.56 EDT Last modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 10.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 45-year-old woman abducted and thrown off a motorway bridge near Florence has become the seventh alleged femicide in Italy since mid-August. Lorena Isceri was abducted on Thursday afternoon, allegedly by her ex-boyfriend, Federico Vella, in the Rifredi area of Florence, before being forced into the boot of his car and driven towards a bridge on the A1 motorway. Isceri, who worked in the veterinary sector, still had her phone and managed to call an emergency helpline, telling operators she had been abducted. Vella, 38, stopped the car, snatched the phone and allegedly threw her off the bridge, before jumping off himself. After Isceri’s call to the helpline, police traced her phone signal but arrived too late to prevent her murder. Officers are establishing whether Isceri was killed before she was thrown off the bridge. Isceri’s mother told SkyTg24 that she had last heard from her daughter on Thursday morning, and said she sounded fine. When asked about the relationship with Vella, she said Isceri had spoken to her about it and was “very afraid”. Italian interior ministry data had indicated a downward trend in femicides during the first six months of 2026. Figures compiled by the feminist alliance Non Una di Meno showed that as of 8 August, 40 women had been killed so far this year. But numbers have risen since 15 August, Italy’s Ferragosto national holiday, with seven women, including Isceri, killed by a current or former partner. Giorgia Meloni’s ruling coalition, which on Friday celebrated becoming the longest-serving government in the history of the Italian republic, had pledged to crack down on gender-based violence after the strong public reaction to the killing of Giulia Cecchetin , a 22-year-old medical student, by her former boyfriend, in November 2023. Two years later, the government approved a law that for the first time introduced a legal definition of femicide in criminal law, punishing it with life in prison, while increasing sentences for crimes including stalking, sexual violence and the sharing of intimate images without consent. However, a campaign to educate schoolboys about healthy relationships was thwarted after the government made it conditional on parental approval. Luisa Rizzitelli, the Italy coordinator of One Billion Rising, which campaigns to end violence against women, said: “Perhaps Meloni is right to celebrate her government’s longevity, because there is precious little to celebrate in terms of concrete results. “The approach to the tragic issue of male violence against women has been based on security policies while completely lacking strategic, structural programmes for training and prevention. The stubborn refusal to implement sex and relationship education in schools is a major factor fuelling the epidemic of femicides in Italy.” In the UK, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123 and the domestic abuse helpline is 0808 2000 247. In the US, the suicide prevention lifeline is 988 and the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is on 13 11 14 and the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. https://www.dw.com/en/voting-to-begin-in.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O2oP Andrej Babis is one of the country's richest people [Photo: 2025] Image: Petr David Josek/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Voters in the Czech Republic begin casting ballots in local polls on Friday to elect local representatives as well as one-third of the Senate's members. The elections are being seen as a test of popularity for the populist billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis. Babis took power last December after forming a coalition with two small political groups. His party, the ANO, or YES, won big in parliamentary elections last year after he was able to tap into people's economic frustration, playing into a sentiment that the center-right government at that time was spending too much on Ukraine. But Babis ran into challenges as well after having formed a government, with the opposition challenging his widening budget deficit — which is when the government spends more than it earns. But he survived a no-confidence vote in parliament earlier this month. Babis, 72, founded the Patriots for Europe in the European Parliament with former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and other far-right parties. Housing shortage is big issue in Czech cities More than 8 million eligible voters are set to elect municipal and town councils in more than 6,200 districts nationwide. Housing shortages, a big theme in major European cities including Berlin and Madrid, is a top concern for voters in the Czech Republic's major cities too. As for the Senate, a third of the seats are up for grabs, as they are every two years. The vote will determine whether the liberal and conservative opposition can retain their majority in the chamber or whether the governing parties and their allies make gains. President Petr Pavel drew attention ahead of the vote because he said he was not going to be able to cast his ballot since he was on a private holiday outside Europe. "The president regrets the planning error," his spokesman said. https://www.odnako.org/jaan-roose-after-.text: International Jaan Roose, after the Strait of Messina the tape 120 meters over Seoul By John 2026-10-02 Estonian acrobat Jaan Roose completed the attempt to cross on a 160 meter long rope suspended 120 meters above the ground, in the center of Seoul, near the city’s famous Gyeongbokgung Palace, between the Hotel Koreana and the Dong-A Media Center. The reports it Guardian . Sitting and lying on the webbing at the halfway point Below him, Seoul traffic continued to flow and the crowd held their breath every time the athlete swayed. Halfway through the course, Roose sat cross-legged on the ribbon and then lay down on his back, arousing the amazement and gasps of those watching from below, before getting up and continuing. Upon reaching the Dong-A Media Center, he turned and began the walk back to the hotel terrace. Upside down above the crowd Halfway, he crouched down again and waved to the crowd. This time, however, he hung from the tape with one arm and then let himself dangle upside down, supported only by his feet. At the end of the performance, the crowd applauded; some spectators appeared visibly relieved. A three-time slackline world champion, the thirty-four-year-old has made a name for himself by performing in spectacular urban settings, such as the feat he accomplished at 185 meters above sea level between the Katara Towers in Qatar. The precedent of the Strait of Messina Roose’s name is also linked to the Strait of Messina. On 10 July 2024, the Estonian athlete crossed the Strait on a slackline, from the Santa Trada pylon, in Villa San Giovanni, to the Torre Faro pylon, in Messina: approximately 3.6 kilometers on a ribbon just 1.9 centimeters wide, suspended over 200 meters above sea level. On this occasion he fell when there were around 80 meters to go; he then resumed the crossing and completed it, but the record was not approved because the regulations required a route without falls.
